subject: Computer Science
summary: Covers business communication and forms of business organisation, the fundamentals of financial accounting (concepts, rules of debit and credit, books, trial balance, depreciation, BRS, bills of exchange), and business economics (demand, elasticity, costs, market structures and RBI monetary policy). These small units give easy marks in DSSSB through direct definition and short calculation questions.

sections.heading: Business communication
sections.body:
**Communication process**: sender → encoding → message → channel → decoding → receiver → **feedback** (noise can disturb any stage).

**Types of business communication**:
- **Internal** - within the organisation: **upward** (subordinate to superior: reports, suggestions), **downward** (superior to subordinate: orders, policies), **lateral/horizontal** (between peers or departments at the same level).
- **External** - with customers, suppliers, government, investors, the public.
- **Formal** (official channels) and **informal** (the **grapevine**, fast but may spread rumours).
- Verbal (oral, written) and non-verbal (body language, gestures).

**7 Cs**: clear, concise, concrete, correct, coherent, complete, courteous. **Barriers**: physical (noise, distance), semantic (language, jargon), psychological (emotions, prejudice), organisational (rigid hierarchy, too many levels), cultural. **Poor communication** of processes makes employees unhappy, which can damage the corporate image and reduce business success.

**Business writing**: letters, memos, notices, circulars, minutes, reports and e-mails. A **proposal** persuades the reader to take action and highlights the benefits of the suggested plan. Notes can be organised for interpretation with flow charts, tables and headings.

sections.heading: Forms of business organisation and management
sections.body:
- **Sole proprietorship** - one owner, **unlimited liability**, easy to form, owner keeps all profit.
- **Partnership** (Indian Partnership Act, 1932) - at least 2 partners, maximum limited under the Companies Act, 2013 rules; based on a partnership deed; generally unlimited liability. **LLP** (Limited Liability Partnership) gives partners limited liability.
- **Joint Hindu Family business** - managed by the Karta.
- **Cooperative society** - voluntary association for mutual benefit, one member one vote.
- **Joint stock company** - artificial person with **separate legal entity**, **limited liability** and **perpetual succession**. **Private company**: minimum 2, maximum 200 members; **public company**: minimum **7** members, no maximum; **One Person Company**: 1 member.

**Types of partners**: **active/working** (invests and manages), **sleeping/dormant** (invests, shares profit, does not take part), **nominal** (only **lends his name**, no capital or profit share, but liable to outsiders), **partner by estoppel** (represents himself as a partner), **secret** partner, **minor** (admitted only to the benefits).

**Functions of management**: **planning, organising, staffing, directing and controlling** (Gulick's POSDCORB adds coordinating, reporting and budgeting). Coding and testing are technical, not managerial, functions. Henri Fayol gave 14 principles of management (division of work, unity of command, scalar chain, etc.).

sections.heading: Accounting: meaning, objectives and concepts
sections.body:
**Accounting** is the process of identifying, measuring, recording, classifying, summarising, analysing and communicating financial information to users. Branches: financial, cost and management accounting.

**Objectives of (financial) accounting**:
- Maintain systematic **records of business transactions**.
- Ascertain **profit or loss** (through the profit and loss account).
- Ascertain the **financial position** (balance sheet).
- **Report** financial information to owners, creditors, government and other users.
- Prevent and detect errors, frauds and **defalcation** (misappropriation) by internal control.

**Basic concepts and conventions**: business entity (business separate from owner), money measurement, going concern, accounting period, historical cost, **dual aspect** (every transaction has two sides), revenue recognition (realisation), matching, accrual, full disclosure, consistency, **conservatism/prudence** (anticipate no profit, provide for all losses), materiality.

**Accounting equation** (from dual aspect): **Assets = Liabilities + Capital**. Double-entry book-keeping (systematised by Luca Pacioli) records every transaction with equal debit and credit.

sections.heading: Rules of debit and credit
sections.body:
Two equivalent approaches: the **traditional (golden) rules** based on the type of account, and the **modern (accounting-equation) rules**.

Under the modern rules: an **increase in assets** or expenses is debited; an **increase in liabilities**, capital or income is credited; a **decrease in an asset is credited** and a decrease in a liability is debited.

**Classification of accounts** (traditional): **personal** (persons, firms, banks, capital, drawings), **real** (assets: cash, machinery, furniture, goodwill), **nominal** (expenses, losses, incomes, gains).

sections.heading: Books of account, trial balance and final accounts
sections.body:
- **Journal** - book of **original (prime) entry**; records transactions in **chronological** order (date-wise) with debit, credit and narration.
- **Ledger** - principal book of **analytical (classified)** record; transactions are **posted** from the journal into individual accounts.
- **Subsidiary books**: cash book (single, double or triple column), purchases book, sales book, purchase returns, sales returns, bills receivable/payable books, journal proper.
- **Balancing**: all **permanent accounts** (assets, liabilities, capital - real and personal) are balanced and carried forward to the next period; **temporary (nominal) accounts** are closed at the end of the period by transfer to the trading or profit and loss account.
- **Trial balance** - list of ledger balances to check **arithmetical accuracy** (total debits = total credits). It cannot reveal errors of omission, errors of principle or compensating errors.
- **Final accounts**: **Trading account** (gross profit = sales − cost of goods sold), **Profit and Loss account** (net profit), **Balance sheet** (assets and liabilities on a date).
- **Capital expenditure** gives long-term benefit (buying machinery); **revenue expenditure** is for day-to-day running (wages, rent).
- **Tally** is a widely used accounting application software.

sections.heading: Depreciation, bank reconciliation and bills of exchange
sections.body:
**Depreciation** is the gradual fall in the value of a fixed asset due to wear and tear, passage of time, obsolescence or depletion.
- **Straight Line Method (SLM / fixed instalment)**: same amount every year = (cost − scrap value) ÷ useful life.
- **Written Down Value (WDV / diminishing balance)**: fixed percentage on the opening book value, so the charge falls each year.

**Bank Reconciliation Statement (BRS)** explains the difference between the cash book (bank column) and the bank passbook. Causes: cheques deposited but **not yet collected**; cheques issued but not yet presented; **interest and dividends collected** by the bank or direct deposits not yet recorded in the cash book; bank charges; dishonoured cheques; errors.

**Bill of exchange**: an unconditional written order by the **drawer** (creditor) directing the **drawee** (debtor) to pay a sum to the **payee**; it is valid once **accepted** by the drawee. Due date = date + term + **3 days of grace**. If the drawee fails to pay on maturity the bill is **dishonoured**. **Discounting** = encashing the bill with a bank before maturity; **endorsement** = transferring it. A **promissory note** is a promise to pay made by the debtor.

sections.heading: Business economics, demand and costs
sections.body:
**Business (managerial) economics** is the discipline that applies economic theory to business management and decision making. **Microeconomics** studies individual units (consumer, firm, price of a good); **macroeconomics** studies the whole economy (national income, inflation, employment). **Positive economics** describes *what is* - factual, verifiable statements that can be proved or disproved; **normative economics** says *what ought to be* (value judgements). A business economist forecasts demand and business conditions after studying internal and external factors, informs management about economic trends, and helps the firm earn a reasonable profit on capital employed.

**Law of demand**: other things equal, quantity demanded rises as price falls (inverse relation). Exceptions: **Giffen goods**, **Veblen (prestige) goods**, expectation of further price rises. As income rises, demand for a **normal good rises** and for an **inferior good falls**. **Price elasticity of demand** Ed = % change in quantity ÷ % change in price; |Ed| > 1 elastic, < 1 inelastic, = 1 unitary. **Law of supply**: quantity supplied rises with price.

**Costs**: TC = TFC + TVC; AC = TC ÷ Q; MC = ΔTC ÷ ΔQ. Because of the law of variable proportions the **short-run MC and AC curves are U-shaped**; MC cuts AVC and AC at their **minimum** points. Profit is maximised where **MR = MC** (with MC rising).

sections.heading: Market structures
sections.body: Markets are classified by the number of sellers, the nature of the product and the firm's control over price. Under **perfect competition** the firm is a price taker, so its demand curve is horizontal and AR = MR. Under **monopoly** and **monopolistic competition** the firm faces a downward-sloping demand curve, so MR lies below AR; in monopolistic competition products are differentiated (brands) and firms spend on advertising (selling costs). In **oligopoly** a few large firms are interdependent, so each must consider rivals' reactions.

sections.heading: Money, banking and RBI monetary policy
sections.body:
**Monetary policy** regulates the supply and cost of money and credit to control inflation and support growth. The Reserve Bank of India (established 1935) issues currency, is banker to the government and **banker's bank**, lender of last resort, custodian of foreign exchange and controller of credit.
- **Quantitative tools**: **CRR** (Cash Reserve Ratio - share of deposits banks must keep as **cash with the RBI**), **SLR** (Statutory Liquidity Ratio - share of deposits banks keep in liquid assets such as cash, gold and approved government securities), **repo rate** (rate at which RBI lends short-term to banks against securities), **reverse repo rate** (rate RBI pays banks for parking funds), **bank rate** (long-term lending rate without repurchase), **Open Market Operations** (buying/selling government securities), MSF and LAF.
- **Selling bonds** in open market operations takes money from banks and the public, **reducing bank reserves and the money supply**; buying bonds increases them. Raising CRR, SLR or repo rate also tightens money supply.
- **Qualitative tools**: **moral suasion** (persuasion and advice to banks), margin requirements, credit rationing, selective credit control, direct action.

formulas.name: SLM depreciation
formulas.formula: Annual depreciation = (Cost − Scrap value) ÷ Useful life

formulas.name: WDV depreciation
formulas.note: Book value falls each year; charge decreases.

formulas.name: Gross and net profit
formulas.formula: GP = Net sales − Cost of goods sold;  NP = GP + other incomes − indirect expenses
formulas.note: Cost of goods sold = Opening stock + Purchases + Direct expenses − Closing stock.

formulas.name: Cost relations
formulas.formula: TC = TFC + TVC;  AC = TC/Q;  MC = TCₙ − TCₙ₋₁
formulas.note: MC cuts AC at its minimum.

formulas.name: Profit maximisation
formulas.note: Under perfect competition this becomes P = MC.

workedExamples.problem: Practice: Pass journal entries and show the effect on the accounting equation: (1) Mohan starts business with cash ₹50,000; (2) buys furniture for cash ₹10,000; (3) buys goods on credit from Ravi ₹8,000; (4) pays rent ₹2,000.
workedExamples.solution:
1. Cash A/c Dr 50,000 / To Capital A/c 50,000 (asset ↑ debit; capital ↑ credit). Assets 50,000 = Liabilities 0 + Capital 50,000.
2. Furniture A/c Dr 10,000 / To Cash A/c 10,000 (real: what comes in Dr, what goes out Cr). Assets unchanged at 50,000.
3. Purchases A/c Dr 8,000 / To Ravi A/c 8,000 (Ravi is the giver, credited). Assets 58,000 = Liabilities 8,000 + Capital 50,000.
4. Rent A/c Dr 2,000 / To Cash A/c 2,000 (nominal: expense Dr). Assets 56,000 = Liabilities 8,000 + Capital 48,000 (expense reduces capital).

workedExamples.problem: Practice: A machine costs ₹1,00,000, scrap value ₹10,000, life 5 years. Find annual depreciation by SLM, and depreciation for 3 years by WDV at 20% p.a.
workedExamples.solution:
SLM = (1,00,000 − 10,000) ÷ 5 = **₹18,000 every year**.
WDV at 20%:
- Year 1: 20% of 1,00,000 = 20,000 → book value 80,000.
- Year 2: 20% of 80,000 = 16,000 → book value 64,000.
- Year 3: 20% of 64,000 = 12,800 → book value **51,200**.
Total WDV depreciation in 3 years = 48,800 (charge falls each year).

workedExamples.problem: Practice: When the price of a good rises from ₹10 to ₹12, quantity demanded falls from 100 to 70 units. Find the price elasticity and say what happens to total spending.
workedExamples.solution:
% change in quantity = (70 − 100) ÷ 100 × 100 = −30%.
% change in price = (12 − 10) ÷ 10 × 100 = 20%.
Ed = −30 ÷ 20 = **−1.5**, |Ed| = 1.5 > 1 → **elastic** demand.
Total expenditure: before 10 × 100 = ₹1,000; after 12 × 70 = ₹840 - it **falls**, as expected when price rises and demand is elastic.

workedExamples.problem: Practice: A firm's TFC is ₹100 and TVC for outputs 1 to 5 is ₹40, 70, 90, 120, 170. Find TC, AC and MC and comment.
workedExamples.solution:
TC = 100 + TVC: 140, 170, 190, 220, 270.
AC = TC ÷ Q: 140, 85, 63.33, 55, 54.
MC = change in TC: 40, 30, 20, 30, 50.
MC falls to a minimum of 20 at Q = 3 and then rises (U-shape). AC keeps falling up to Q = 5 because MC is still below AC (50 < 55); AC would start rising only once MC exceeds it.

pitfalls: Journal = chronological record (book of prime entry); ledger = analytical/classified record.
Decrease in an asset is credited; increase in a liability is credited.
Nominal accounts are closed at year end; real and personal (permanent) accounts are carried forward.
A nominal partner only lends his name; a sleeping partner invests money but does not take part.
Public company needs at least 7 members; private company at least 2.
SLM gives a constant charge; WDV gives a decreasing charge.
Inferior good: demand falls when income rises; normal good: demand rises.
Under monopolistic competition the demand curve slopes downward; a horizontal curve is perfect competition.
CRR is kept as cash with RBI; SLR is kept by banks themselves in liquid assets. Moral suasion is qualitative.
quickRevision: Internal communication: upward, downward, lateral; grapevine is informal.
Management functions: planning, organising, staffing, directing, controlling.
Objectives of accounting: records, profit/loss, financial position, reporting, prevent fraud.
Golden rules: personal - receiver/giver; real - comes in/goes out; nominal - expenses/incomes.
Trial balance checks arithmetical accuracy only.
Bill of exchange: drawer, drawee, payee; 3 days of grace; failure to pay = dishonour.
Depreciation methods: straight line and written down value.
Positive economics = what is (verifiable); normative = what ought to be.
Short-run MC is U-shaped and cuts AC at its minimum.
OMO sale of bonds reduces bank reserves and money supply.
RBI tools: CRR, SLR, repo, reverse repo, bank rate, OMO; qualitative: moral suasion.
